episodes.171396: A mild and moist airmass in advance of an arriving mid level trough of low pressure and nose of an upper level jet favored an environment conducive for severe thunderstorms across coastal waters.
episodes.171397: A couple of thunderstorms produced localized downbursts resulting in tree damage.
episodes.171398: An isolated strong thunderstorm produced gusty winds over the upper Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.171459: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to parts of New Jersey on August 22.  Rainfall totals were as high as 3 to nearly 6 inches.
episodes.171787: Showers and thunderstorms developed near a boundary during the afternoon and evening of the 21st as well as the 22nd. Anomalous moisture was present, and the storm motion was slow which led to areas of flooding and flash flooding.
episodes.172078: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the afternoon as a result of heating beneath an upper-level trough. Fairly steep mid-level lapse rates combined with surface heating resulted in CAPE increasing to near 1000 J/kg. Cells were generally quick-moving, but a multi-cell segment moving eastward was positioned just right such that localized flooding occurred in New Florence PA.
episodes.172183: A tropical wave moved across the area, increasing convergence at the lower levels. Later in the period, low level moisture was provided by the proximity of a surface trough. Additionally, an upper level low approached from the northeast, providing instability aloft, as high pressure at all level weakened.
episodes.172219: Unsettled weather conditions due to an upper level trough generated streamers from Vieques toward eastern Puerto Rico. A waterspout was spotted from these streamers.
episodes.172374: A low pressure system and attendant cold front worked its way through the Ohio Valley on August 21st and into West Virginia. An abundance of moisture was already in place ahead of the frontal passage, which allowed for showers and storms ahead of the front to dump heavy downpours across northeastern West Virginia. Strong to severe storms progressed east of the Ohio River by the afternoon of  the 21st, resulting in a few downed trees in Jackson County and Nicholas County. The threat then transitioned over to flash flooding as heavy downpours prevailed. Localized high water issues arose on roadways in the state that evening into the early morning hours of August 22nd, with one instance of a bridge washing out.
episodes.172526: Generally west steering flow along with deep moisture (PWATs 2 inches or more) and impulses of energy in this flow aloft triggered numerous showers and storms during the afternoon and evening hours. Westerly flow pinned the Atlantic coast sea breeze to the coast and gave an early start to the Gulf coast sea breeze shifting inland across northeast Florida. Strong thunderstorms developed in the afternoon as they interacted with the stationary Atlantic sea breeze boundary along the coast before shifting offshore. These storms produced gusts between 45 to 55 mph at Marineland, St. Augustine and Mayport. Also, lightning struck a house in Neptune beach causing a house fire. Street flooding and heavy rain in Jacksonville Beach and Clay county were caused by training storms moving northeastward along a line that set up extending from Jacksonville Beach to Ocala.
episodes.172822: Showers and thunderstorms developed out ahead of an approaching cold front. Storm coverage and intensity increased as a potent shortwave lifted through the region. Severe storms around the Lehigh Valley formed in the vicinity of a warm front that was bisecting the region.
episodes.172823: Showers and thunderstorms developed out ahead of an approaching cold front. Storm coverage and intensity increased as a potent shortwave lifted through the region. Severe storms around the Lehigh Valley and North Jersey formed in the vicinity of a warm front that was bisecting the region.
episodes.173013: A cold front moved into a warm, moist airmass and generated thunderstorms. Some of these storms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
episodes.173130: Showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a low pressure system moving through the Ohio Valley.
episodes.173247: A slow-moving upper trough combined with a stalling front, and a large swath of tropical moisture, to produce record and near-record rainfall across parts of North Texas late August 21 through August 22. Considerable flooding occurred across Dallas County after upwards of 15 inches of rain fell in some areas. Numerous roads, vehicles, homes, buildings and more were flooded and heavily damaged by this event. Damage assessments indicate over 800 buildings and homes were impacted by flood waters, and many were under insured. Preliminary reports indicated 27 destroyed buildings and nearly 300 with major damage. One fatality was reported during this event when a vehicle was swept off a road by a nearby creek.
episodes.173332: A warm front, drifting northward from the Carolinas across the lower Mid-Atlantic, triggered scattered thunderstorms with heavy rain.  Strong heating during the afternoon supported surface-based CAPE values rising into the 2,000 to 2,500 J/Kg range, while precipitable water values ranged from around 1.5 inches along the Blue Ridge to in excess of 1.8 inches across the central Piedmont of Virginia and North Carolina.  Wind speeds through 700 mb were generally around 10 knots, supporting slow cell movement that would contribute to prolonged heavy rainfall over some locations. Many of the storms produced rainfall at 3 to 5 inch per hour rates, which resulted in flash flooding of small streams in the local area.
episodes.173336: Another period of moderate to heavy rainfall, forced the closure of Highway 125.  The highway was closed in both directions for several hours due to safety concerns regarding mudslides.
episodes.173414: A cold front stalled across Texas, Arkansas and through Tennessee. This boundary provided an unstable atmosphere as far south of the northern Gulf Coast. Local precipitable water values were very high, well in excess of 2 inches. Thus, the environment was primed for widespread convection. One of those storms along the Mississippi Sound was able to intensify enough to produce a waterspout.
episodes.173431: Slow moving thunderstorms that developed along a warm front on August 22nd produced heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding in New Jersey. The thunderstorms developed in an environment with PWATs increasing from 1.6 to 1.9 inches and CAPE values around 2000 J/kg. The storms quickly dropped 1 to 2 inches of rainfall in less than 90 minutes over portions of urban Northeast New Jersey that resulted in localized flash flooding.
episodes.173465: Generally west steering flow along with deep moisture (PWATs 2 inches or more) and impulses of energy in this flow aloft triggered numerous showers and storms during the afternoon and evening hours. Westerly flow pinned the Atlantic coast sea breeze to the coast and gave an early start to the Gulf coast sea breeze shifting inland across northeast Florida. Strong thunderstorms developed in the afternoon as they interacted with the stationary Atlantic sea breeze boundary along the coast before shifting offshore. These storms produced gusts between 45 to 55 mph at Marineland, St. Augustine and Mayport. Also, lightning struck a house in Neptune beach causing a house fire. Street flooding and heavy rain in Jacksonville Beach and Clay county were caused by training storms moving northeastward along a line that set up extending from Jacksonville Beach to Ocala.
episodes.173539: A large upper trough shifted southeast into the Four State Region on August 21st through the 22nd, along the backside of an upper level low pressure system over the Great Lakes. This trough slowed as it entered the region, and interacted with rich Gulf moisture and available heating to help focus scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across the area. Given the weak steering currents aloft, these thunderstorms were slow moving and were very efficient rainfall producers, which resulted in flash flooding across several areas in East Texas, where widespread rainfall amounts of three to six inches fell with isolated higher amounts over seven inches.
episodes.173540: A large upper low pressure system moved into the Great Lakes region on August 22nd, with a trailing upper trough extending southwest of this low into the Southern Plains. This trough induced surface low development along a weak surface boundary across North Texas, and focused areas of showers and embedded thunderstorms over much of the Four State Region. Weak surface heating near this boundary contributed to modestly unstable conditions within a moist environment in place, with enough low level shear available which resulted in a low topped supercell developing near Winona in Northeast Smith County Texas. This storm produced a brief EF-1 tornado which just missed the Winona Independent School District campus, but still downed numerous trees along its path before lifting.
episodes.173687: Numerous days of heavy rain raised levels of the Gila River to moderate or greater flooding levels.  A creek that feeds the Gila River also experienced flooding and caused a bridge on Highway 180 to collapse.
episodes.173708: A stationary thunderstorm stayed over the area for several hours and produced significant amount of rain over the area.
episodes.173803: Persistent moist monsoonal flow fueled thunderstorms over northwest Arizona. Several storms produced flash flooding and severe weather.
episodes.173804: Persistent moist monsoonal flow fueled scattered thunderstorms over southern Nevada. A few storms produced severe weather.
episodes.173821: Heavy rain upstream in New Mexico caused the Gila River to flood at Duncan, where Highway 70 was closed, and several homes and a couple businesses experienced minor flooding. Downstream at Solomon, the bridge was partially flooded.
episodes.173833: A line of thunderstorms developed over the mountains and moved southeast into central Virginia in the late afternoon and early evening hours on August 22, producing gusty wind.
episodes.173842: Flash flooding in several national parks and severe hail were observed with scattered thunderstorms.
episodes.173891: Similar to the 20th, thunderstorms once again initiated across the northern Arizona high terrain during the afternoon of the 21st, though more focused along the Mogollon Rim compared to the day prior. Increased steering flow allowed for thunderstorms to move off of the Rim and toward the lower elevations. High instability (MUCAPE 2,000-2,500 J/kg) helped thunderstorms maintain intensity as they travelled toward the lower deserts. Given the greater steering flow, faster thunderstorm motion helped abate flash flood impacts. Greater shear across northwest Arizona allowed an organized complex of thunderstorms to develop during the evening hours before progressing through southwest Arizona and the Lower Colorado River Valley area, producing severe wind gusts and dense blowing dust into the early morning hours on the 22nd. No injuries were reported.
episodes.173892: An organized complex of strong to severe thunderstorms pushed from northwest Arizona down through the Lower Colorado River Valley area late in the night on the 21st and into the early morning hours on the 22nd. Thunderstorms maintained their intensity as they pushed through far eastern Riverside County, with adequate instability in place. Severe wind gusts and dense blowing dust were observed in Blythe with these thunderstorms. No injuries were reported.
episodes.173954: Thunderstorms in northwest Florida produced lightning which resulted in and injury.
episodes.173992: Deep monsoon moisture over northern Arizona and a trough of low pressure passing through Utah made for a rather active day across the area.  Thunderstorms produce heavy rain, high winds, and small hail.

An EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 95 mph touched down just south of County Road 345 on the west side of Winona. There, it lofted a small metal outbuilding, throwing it across the road, while also uprooting a tree. It continued on to clip the Winona Independent School District campus, where it lifted a training sled as it crossed the football field and damaged the roof of a dugout. The tornado just missed hitting the school buildings by only around 200 yards. The tornado continued on to hit another small metal outbuilding, rolling and destroying it before crossing FM 16. The tornado then paralleled Hussey Circle, downing several more large branches and snapping a large tree which fell into a home. Additional hardwood trees were uprooted as it crossed County Road 155, where the tornado reached its widest point before lifting shortly thereafter.
